articles.title_orig: Netanyahu takes UN stage with one eye on Israel’s election
articles.title_zh: Netanyahu takes UN stage with one eye on Israel’s election
articles.content_orig:
Palestinian leader gives video address after being denied US visa and tells world: ‘Do not allow another Nakba’
Benjamin Netanyahu is set to deliver a controversial address to the United Nations on Thursday just hours after Palestinian leader Mahmoud Abbas said his delegation was “unlawfully” denied visas by the Trump administration to attend the meeting of world leaders.
Street protests have already begun in New York City as the Israeli prime minister arrives on a lightning 12-hour visit where he is expected to give a defiant speechin which he will reject criticism over Israel’s war in Gaza and the expansion of settlements in the West Bank.
Allies previewing the speech suggested it would read both as an address to his rightwing allies in the United States, as well as a defense of his record as prime minister ahead of October elections that could oust him from power.
In a video address from Ramallah, broadcast in the General Assembly Hall, Abbas condemned Israel’s policies in Gaza, the West Bank and East Jerusalem as a “malicious colonial plan” to establish a “‘Greater Israel’ and erase the Palestinian presence”.
Citing the humanitarian crisis in Gaza and the violent expansion of settlements in the West Bank, Abbas said that the Israeli government “now threatens the very life and existence of the Palestinian people in their homeland”.
“Do not allow another Nakba and further massacres like those of 1948 to continue taking place,” he added, referring to the expulsion of Palestinians upon the founding of Israel.
For the second year in a row, the US state department denied visas to Abbas and the Palestinian Authority delegation, arguing that they had failed to live up to their commitments to seek peace with Israel.
“As a consequence of their failure to reform, contrary to their commitments to the United States, and their ongoing activities that undermine the prospects for peace, the United States will extend sanctions that deny visas to PLO members and PA officials,” the state department said last week in a statement.
In his speech, Abbas said his delegation “[rejects] these unlawful punitive measures, as well as the accusations and justifications on which they were based”.
He said: “Preventing the Palestinian delegation from reaching United Nations headquarters is inconsistent with the obligations of the United States as the host country.”
As he spoke, protests were already forming on the streets of New York City near the United Nations headquarters in advance of Netanyahu’s arrival before a speech tentatively scheduled for 2pm ET.
Hundreds of demonstrators crowded into the street on Manhattan’s east side in midtown and held signs that said “End the Genocide” and wore shirts reading “Fund people not bombs”.
Earlier this summer, the mayor, Zohran Mamdani, had said that Netanyahu was “not welcome” in New York, and said he was reviewing whether Netanyahu could be arrested by city police under an international criminal court warrant for his arrest.
He has since tempered that stance, saying this week that he wouldn’t attend the protests but promising to protect their “right to [protest] in this city”.
Israel’s ambassador to the UN, Danny Danon, said in an interview that he believed Mamdani’s new stance was “too little and too late”.
“You know, he set the fire, and now he’s coming to try to calm down the situation,” Danon said ahead of the speech.
Netanyahu is not expected to meet Donald Trump, who is in Washington to host the Chinese leader, Xi Jinping, nor with other senior US officials, as he faces growing international condemnation over his hardline stance. Netanyahu has said that he needs to return to Israel quickly because of the election campaign and the holiday of Sukkot, which begins on Friday.
Palestinian representatives are calling for diplomatic missions to bring staff for a planned walkout of Netanyahu’s speech to “send a clear message to Netanyahu and his government that no one is willing to aid, abet, or be complicit in its genocide and war crimes and illegal occupation, which all peace-loving states and peoples demand must come to an end”.

articles.title_orig: Trump says he and Xi held 'great meeting' as Chinese leader visits White House
articles.title_zh: Trump says he and Xi held 'great meeting' as Chinese leader visits White House
articles.content_orig:
A red carpet and military flyover - How Trump welcomed Xi
US President Donald Trump has been blunt about his AI ambitions, as well as about who he considers the US's main rival to be: China.
His Chinese counterpart, Xi Jinping, has not said anything so forthright - but it seems he holds a similar view.
"China very much sees it as a race, they very much think China should be the leading force in AI - they see AI as a power maximiser," says Rebecca Arcesati, from the Mercator Institute for China Studies.
You can look beyond the rhetoric for evidence of this: AI has been a cornerstone of China's technological ambitions for more than a decade, whether Xi emphasises it publicly or not.
For Trump, beating China to AI supremacy outweighs any risks of the technology to humans - something he has described as "a hoax" .
China's foreign ministry warned that " narratives of threat " and confrontation hinder global AI governance, calling for cooperation to ensure it benefits all.
It means when the two presidents sit down on Thursday there will be few more important topics than their AI ambitions - and what they say and decide will matter to the whole world.
The US and China are locked in a race to develop AI
There's no doubt the US and China are global leaders in AI but who is ahead depends on how success is measured.
American companies lead on so-called frontier models, with the highest-performing systems on most benchmarks coming from firms such as Anthropic, Google and OpenAI.
In February 2025, an AI model by China's DeepSeek "briefly matched the top US model" and as of March 2026, Anthropic's top model led the pack "by just 2.7%", according to researchers at Stanford University , external .
Part of the US advantage stems from the vast sums being invested in leading AI companies as the frontier labs burn through mountains of cash to build the infrastructure to train new models.
OpenAI boss Sam Altman called for a coordinated slowdown of advanced AI development
The stock market is booming and a large part of the US economy's expansion relies on the enormous growth - and projected profitability - of AI companies.
So that might partly explain why President Trump sees AI as key to US success .
Another factor limiting China's ability is the sweeping government restrictions placed on US companies that prevent them from selling advanced microchips to Chinese firms - these are crucial for developing cutting-edge models.
Despite the chip restrictions, new AI models are coming out almost monthly in both countries and it's unclear what "winning" the AI race would actually mean, or whether there is a finish line at all.
Many companies are racing to develop artificial general intelligence (AGI), a theoretical form of AI capable of learning, reasoning and performing a wide range of tasks at or above the level of humans.
The Chinese AI industry has so far focused not on creating frontier models but releasing what is known as open weight models - downloadable and tweakable in a similar way to open source software.
This contrasts with the approach taken by many US firms, which largely focus on proprietary models accessed through paid subscriptions or company platforms.
Chinese open weight models are being released at a rapid pace, with benchmarks showing the country's top models trailing US rivals by only a few months.
Models such as Moonshot AI's Kimi K3 have become popular in China and overseas because they perform close to the frontier models while remaining freely downloadable and adaptable.
Beijing's focus is more about deploying the technology across its economy, China analyst Lizzi Lee from the Asia Society Policy Institute said.
"AI isn't the moon landing," she said. "The US may lead at the frontier, while China could still gain enormous economic and geopolitical leverage by making capable AI cheap, open and ubiquitous."
Yang Zhilin co-founded Moonshot, one of China's most successful AI models, in 2023
AI is also very energy hungry, and China is very well placed there, Rebecca Arcesati told Tech Life on the BBC World Service.
"Chinese AI companies are able to access the electricity they need for a much lower cost and that really is an advantage," she said.
In robotics - a field of AI that some believe will be world-changing - China has become the world's biggest manufacturer of robots , with more than two million working in the country's factories, the International Federation of Robotics estimated.
The nation is also the world's biggest maker of humanoid robots, accounting for more than nine-tenths of global shipments in the first half of the year, according to independent policy institute Chatham House.
Chinese AI developers have showed "remarkable resilience and innovation" in spite of the shortage of advanced American chips, analyst Lian Jye Su from tech research firm Omdia said.
But US officials and AI firms have also alleged that Chinese developers closed the gap by using distillation - a technique that enables models to learn from more advanced platforms.
China's foreign ministry said in response that AI development was "fuelled" by the country's "vision of extensive consultation and joint contribution for shared benefit".
China and the US may be in fierce competition, but their governments' approaches to safety concerns are markedly different.
While some in the industry have recently warned that AI could pose an existential risk to humanity, Chinese researchers seem less concerned about that and are more worried about potential misuse of the technology and cyber war.
Responding to concerns over AI, Trump has said the US already has sufficient rules in place and that the only guardrails AI needs are a "high IQ" president.
"We're leading now over China by a lot, and everyone else, and we're going to keep it that way," Trump said this week, adding that the US was not going to "stifle the growth of something that will be bigger than the industrial revolution".
Washington has prioritised innovation and sought to reduce regulation in an effort to "keep American labs ahead", said information security officer Jayant Dave from cybersecurity firm Check Point Software Technologies.
China is the world's biggest manufacturer of robots
Beijing has taken a different strategy to the US hands-off approach.
Xi urged the country's leaders to keep a close eye on AI's risks and ensure the technology was always "under human control".
"China has taken a relatively cautious and centrally-coordinated approach," introducing guides on data usage and algorithms before many other countries, helping to address many underlying concerns, Dave said.
The use of guidelines, though not legally binding, sets expectations while giving developers room to innovate, said National University of Singapore AI ethics lecturer Jonathan Sim.
Despite calls for international cooperation, it remains unclear how the AI superpowers plan to address the technology's potential dangers - if at all.
The two countries have previously cooperated on existential threats such as nuclear weapons, but that was based on a shared understanding of the threat, which is not currently the case with AI, Dave said.
"Washington worries about capability escaping control. Beijing worries about capability threatening domestic stability," he added.
Trump has dismissed proposals for an industry-wide slowdown, arguing that it could allow Chinese developers to close the gap.
Ahead of the Trump-Xi summit, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng discussed establishing a notification mechanism for serious AI incidents.
While the messaging from Trump on China in recent weeks has been "more antagonistic", the fact that AI is expected to be on the agenda was a "good start", said policy analyst Leia Wang from the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace.
What we don't want, she added, was for an "unhealthy version of the race narrative to perpetuate", potentially escalating an already fierce rivalry in AI.

articles.title_orig: CNN, MS NOW and Politico allowed back at the White House after judge blocked Trump’s ban
articles.title_zh: CNN, MS NOW and Politico allowed back at the White House after judge blocked Trump’s ban
articles.content_orig:
The outlets had requested an emergency hearing after the White House initially seemed to flout a judge’s order
US politics live – latest updates
Journalists for CNN, MS Now and Politico were finally granted access to the White House on Thursday afternoon, many hours after a federal judge had ruled that the Trump administration must allow them back in after imposing a ban.
Earlier attempts by the journalists to enter the building had been unsuccessful, and lawyers representing the three organizations had told a judge that the White House has already “repeatedly violated” his overnight order requiring the Trump administration to return the press badges of journalists from the three news organizations.
Timothy Kelly, the US district judge who appeared skeptical of arguments from lawyers representing the White House during a hearing on Wednesday, issued an early morning order forcing the administration to return access for a 14-day period.
But journalists from the three affected networks reported being barred from the building, with some having their badges taken for the first time.
“This morning journalists from each of CNN, MS Now , and Politico attempted to enter the White House and were turned away, and Secret Service agents confiscated the hard pass of journalists whose hard passes had not previously been confiscated,” lawyers for the three news organizations wrote in a brief requesting a video or telephone conference “as soon as possible this morning”.
In a legal filing on Thursday afternoon, Micah Stopperich, the White House director of press operations, said in a sworn statement that the operations team was notified at 7.10am to restore access, and that it began reinstating badges at 7.25am. She said that US Secret Service indicated that badges were re-activated as of 9.07am, and that confiscated badges were dropped off at the entry to the building just before 10am.
“United States Secret Service has represented that press passes that were turned on were available for pick up at the press gate as soon as they were delivered,” she said.
The badges were revoked on Saturday, after the president abruptly ordered the three outlets to be banned over “their constant ‘reporting’ FAKE NEWS”. The outlets swiftly sued over the move, which sparked widespread criticism from other news organizations and press freedom advocates.
In a legal filing earlier this week, Department of Justice lawyers argued that the ban was necessary for national security reasons, and listed examples of articles that relied on non-public information.
But Kelly was unswayed, and argued in his ruling that the way in the which the White House banned the organizations had likely violated due process protections for journalists – and well-established legal precedent set in two press access cases by the United States court of appeals for the District of Columbia.
“Plaintiffs are also likely to succeed in showing that their hard passes were revoked without constitutionally adequate due process,” he wrote. “The ‘general rule’ is that ‘individuals must receive notice and an opportunity to be heard before the government deprives them’ of a constitutionally protected interest.”
The judge said that, based on case law, before a press pass can be revoked, the White House “must promulgate rules or standards governing the conduct that would lead to such revocation. And the reporter must ‘receive fair notice not only of the conduct that would subject him to punishment, but also of the magnitude of the sanction that the White House might impose’.”
The three news organizations were not given advance notice that they were in violation of any set of standards and only received formal notice – in letters sent to each news organization on Tuesday – that they “exhibited behavior in violation of the standards of professionalism and decorum expected of those given access to the White House Complex, including by trafficking in verifiable falsehoods about national security and other issues, and publishing sensitive or classified information”.
Michael Kenneth Velchik, a justice department attorney representing the Trump White House, argued that such a process had been laid out in the letters, which informed each news organization that they had until 5pm on Friday to contest the ban. (The letters said that if the organizations did not submit such a challenge, it would become final.)
But the judge said the standard mentioned in the letters was “so vague it hardly does the trick”, and concluded that even the defendants “do not dispute that plaintiffs did not receive notice and an opportunity to be heard before their hard passes were revoked”.
The judge also wrote that he was “skeptical … that defendants’ interest in safeguarding national security is the actual motivation for, or is even advanced by, the revocation of Plaintiffs’ hard passes”. He cited comments from Trump about how the ban was for content-based reasons.
A hearing for a preliminary injunction will be expedited to be held during the 14-day period in which the passes are returned, the judge said.
Theodore J Boutrous Jr, an attorney for CNN , MS Now and Politico, praised the judge’s determination. “This is a strong ruling vindicating freedom of the press, due process and the rule of law,” he said in a statement. “We greatly appreciate the court’s swift action.”
Seemingly anticipating a loss, Trump already said in a post on Truth Social earlier this week that the White House would appeal any adverse ruling.

articles.title_orig: Global bond selloff deepens, as US 30-year yields hit highest since 2004
articles.title_zh: Global bond selloff deepens, as US 30-year yields hit highest since 2004
articles.content_orig:
Treasury yields were trading at multidecade highs on Thursday, as investor bets on another rate hike from the Federal Reserve mounted.
The 30-year Treasury bond yield was up 5 basis points 5.456% and reached a 2004 peak. The benchmark 10-year Treasury note yield , which is tied to rates on mortgages, rose more than 4 basis points to 5.162% and hit its highest level since July 2007. The yield on the 2-year note gained more than 1 basis point to 4.908% and remained close to a 2023 high.
One basis point equals 0.01%, and yields and prices move in opposite directions.
Global bonds also sold off. Japan's 10-year JGB yield rose its highest since August 1996. U.K. Gilts and German Bunds also moved higher, with yields on various European bonds hitting fresh multi-year highs.
Thursday's moves build on a U.S. Treasury rout that took place Wednesday. The 10-year Treasury yield had its biggest one-day jump since April 7, 2025 as traders reacted to stronger-than-expected U.S. economic data, hawkish commentary from a Federal Reserve official and high oil prices.
"The combination of fiscal, economic, geopolitical, and supply-side inflation pressures converging has bond markets in less familiar territory. The recent rise in yields can no longer be attributed simply to concerns over the deficit," said from Mike Sanders, head of fixed income at Madison Investments.
The data drove expectations of more rate hikes, with traders last pricing in a more-than-75 % chance that the Federal Open Market Committee will increase rates again at its October meeting, per the CME Group's FedWatch tool . That compares to a roughly 49% probability just a week ago.
"With markets pricing in four rate hikes through next year, the Fed is being pushed toward tighter policy at a time when the risk of a policy mistake is rising," he added.
Michael Barr, a member of the Fed's Board of Governors, said in a speech on Wednesday that "further policy adjustments" are likely to come to bring inflation down to target. Speaking in London on Thursday, New York Federal Reserve President John Williams said it would be "reasonable" to expect another Fed interest rate hike by the end of the year.

articles.title_orig: US citizen injured in Illinois after ICE agents mistook him for fugitive and tried to arrest him
articles.title_zh: US citizen injured in Illinois after ICE agents mistook him for fugitive and tried to arrest him
articles.content_orig:
Man left bloodied and hurt after immigration enforcement agents tried to arrest him in Evanston, a Chicago suburb
An eyewitness has described how two federal immigration agents allegedly beat and badly injured a US citizen in a botched arrest attempt in Illinois , and left the man dazed and bleeding on the ground as they walked away after realizing their apparent mistake.
Bystander Ryan Garton told the Associated Press that he saw the agents pinning down the man, who is Black, on the side of the road as he was driving home on Sunday in Evanston, a suburb of Chicago. He said he pulled over to record what was happening on video.
“His upper right eye socket and temple were swollen as if he had been punched,” Garton said. The man’s face, he added, was scraped “as if it had been ground into the sidewalk”.
Garton, 56, said one agent had his knee on the man’s back and was “beating up on him”, even as the person shouted: “I’m a citizen, leave me alone.” The witness said about five people were standing nearby, yelling at the agents to stop.
Garton said he urged the officer to get off the man so he could inspect his injuries, and also asserted that the officer acknowledged that he was already aware the man was a US citizen. When the agent stepped away, Garton said he saw bloodstains in the shape of handprints on the man’s shirt.
The man told Garton that he had been walking to a pharmacy to pick up a prescription when the agents stopped him.
Another eyewitness, Michael Lipson, the owner of a store across the street from where the incident occurred, said he saw the federal officers wrestle the man to the ground as the alleged victim repeatedly yelled that he was a citizen. The man’s face looked “badly messed up”, Lipson told the AP.
Lipson said the officers checked cards and papers from the man’s wallet before leaving them scattered on the road. Lipson said he laid out his sweatshirt for the man to rest on while Garton inspected his injuries.
Authorities in Illinois said earlier this week they were looking into the incident , which ended with the victim in hospital with injuries to his head, neck and teeth. It also left one of the agents with a bloodied hand that he told Evanston police he sustained while the suspect resisted an effort to handcuff him.
The Department of Homeland Security (DHS), which oversees the Immigration and Customs Enforcement ( ICE ) agency, said in a statement that ICE officers had “encountered an individual who resembled the target” of an enforcement operation.
“The individual was given lawful commands but was not cooperative and refused to identify himself,” the statement said, adding that the agents “left the scene without further incident” after the man said who he was.
“When ICE officers offered the individual assistance, he refused.”
More detailed accounts of the confrontation, which took place at about 10am on Sunday, have come mostly from the city’s police department and local officials.

A police statement said the alleged victim told officers that he received head, face and neck injuries during the beating. It said the agents walked away because they claimed a crowd had gathered and they feared protesters would attack them.
Daniel Biss, the Democratic mayor of Evanston, said in a post on X that the man was treated at St Francis hospital for minor injuries, and that the city’s police department “continues to investigate the situation, and we will remain vigilant about federal activities”.
In a separate post on Wednesday, Biss condemned Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown, which has escalated through the president’s second term with enforcement “surges” into Democratic-run cities and states in particular , and resulted in a record 50,000 arrests in July alone.
“This violence must end. We need to take Evanston’s energy and fight to Washington to abolish ICE, hold the Trump administration accountable, and end the funding of these brutal invasions into our cities,” Biss wrote.
The incident was one of three separate violent events Sunday involving federal immigration officers. In Austin, Texas, an ICE agent shot and seriously wounded a 28-year-old Venezuelan man in a traffic stop while he worked as a DoorDash delivery driver.
In Michigan, authorities are investigating the death of a 36-year-old Guatemalan national who crashed his car into a tree at high speed after reportedly attempting to flee immigration officers that were trying to detain him.
The Associated Press contributed reporting

articles.title_orig: Denmark expects Russia to escalate hybrid warfare in coming months, intelligence service says
articles.title_zh: Denmark expects Russia to escalate hybrid warfare in coming months, intelligence service says
articles.content_orig:
Warning comes hours after Poland says fire at Starlink satellite station was ‘act of sabotage’
Russia could launch a limited military attack against a Nato country in the coming months, Danish intelligence said, in one of the starkest warnings yet by western security services.
In a report published on Thursday, the Danish defence intelligence service warned of a “low but growing risk” that Russia could launch long-range strikes on Nato infrastructure supporting Ukraine , or carry out a limited incursion into a neighbouring country with a small number of troops, potentially operating without insignia.
The report came hours after a fire at a Starlink satellite station in central Poland that local authorities described as an “act of sabotage”.
Krzysztof Gawkowski, the deputy prime minister of Poland, said the blaze, which broke out overnight in the Masovian voivodeship, had been “deliberately designed to disable the station”, disrupting internet access for a number of institutions, including the Ukrainian military.
Gawkowski said it had not been established who ​was responsible for the fire, but that “many signs suggest this aligns with Russia’s new ‌doctrine ⁠of attack.
“While everything is operational today, we must recognise, as prime minister [Donald] Tusk recently noted, that this is an element of hybrid warfare,” he said.
Starlink has become a key part of Ukraine’s military communications, and the incident comes amid a spate of suspected Russian sabotage operations across European infrastructure supporting Ukraine.
Earlier this month, Germany publicly blamed Russia for an attempted drone attack on Leipzig/Halle airport, while a series of other incidents – including fires at drone factories and sabotage targeting rail infrastructure – have also been investigated for possible links to Moscow. Russia has denied involvement in such attacks.
In recent weeks, several European intelligence chiefs have warned that Russia may be preparing more assertive actions to test Nato countries’ commitment to supporting Ukraine, though officials differ over how imminent such a move may be.
Russia is expected to intensify its hybrid attacks against European countries with “greater consequences” for those targeted in the coming months, the Danes warned, including “destructive cyber-attacks that cripple societal functions as well as sabotage attacks that carry a high risk of casualties”.
A source familiar with Moscow’s thinking agreed that Russia was likely to step up its hybrid attacks.
“Russian military top command is convinced some Nato countries are directly involved in the war against Russia – not just by supplying Ukraine with weapons and intelligence, but by helping to guide missiles and drones,” the source said, speaking on condition of anonymity.
“They therefore believe Nato is already waging a hybrid war against Russia, and that Russia has the right to respond in kind,” the source added.
“Hybrid attacks” are broad terms generally used to describe non-military tactics aimed at pressuring or destabilising an adversary, including cyber-attacks, sabotage and disinformation.
The aim of Russia’s actions would be to divert European resources away from supporting Ukraine, and deepen divisions within Nato if the alliance failed to agree on a collective response, the report added.
The service believes it remained “highly unlikely” that Russia would launch an outright invasion of a Nato country, but notably said it “cannot be ruled out”.
The Danish services said Russia could seek to test Nato’s article 5, which commits members to collective defence. They warned there was “a risk that Russia assesses that the Nato countries will not respond collectively”, particularly if Moscow believes the US is unable or unwilling to support its European allies in a potential war with Russia.
There have been ongoing jitters among Nato members over whether the alliance’s most powerful member, the US, would come to Europe’s defence under Donald Trump in the event of a Russian attack.
Questions over unity within Europe are also growing. Last week, Slovakia’s prime minister, Robert Fico, who has maintained close ties with the Kremlin, cast doubt on his country’s commitment to Nato’s collective defence principle, saying he did not want Slovakia drawn into a military conflict “because of some article 5”.
Speaking at the UN general assembly on Wednesday, Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned that Russia continued to threaten countries beyond Ukraine, including Moldova, Poland and the Baltic states, while showing “no respect” for the sovereignty of countries in the south Caucasus and central Asia.
“The more freedom Putin has to act, the more dangerous the world becomes for everyone else,” he said.

articles.content_orig:
Macklemore performs at the Goldencoast Rap Festival in Corcelles-les-Monts, near Dijon, central-eastern France, on 30 August, 2026
Rapper Macklemore is launching a "Free Palestine" tour, days after being dropped from Ed Sheeran's Loop Tour following pro-Palestinian comments he made  onstage earlier this month.
"So, as you all know, my schedule freed up a bit," he said upon announcing the tour on Thursday.
The American artist - whose real name is Benjamin Haggerty - said proceeds from the tour, which launches in Dublin next month, will go to organisations supporting Palestinians.
Macklemore's onstage comments and subsequent removal from the tour led Sheeran's support acts to drop out, while the British singer stressed that the decision to drop the rapper was made by his promoter, not by himself.
Everything we know about the Ed Sheeran and Macklemore controversy
In a statement on Thursday, the rapper said that the last couple of weeks had shown him there had been "a collective awakening around Palestinian liberation, the power of billionaires that try to censor that call, and what we expect from artists right now".
"What happened to me is bigger than one artist or one stage," he said. "When the billionaire class can decide which voices are allowed on stage and which ones are too dangerous to hear, everyone should be paying attention."
Macklemore said he had spent the last week contacting artists who had used their platforms to stand in solidarity with the Palestinian people, regardless of the consequences.
Due to how quickly the tour came together, several details were still being worked out, he added: "But this is a moment of momentum, and there is work to be done."
Macklemore's new tour will begin in Dublin on 26 October followed by Paris on 29 October and London on 30 October.
US dates will also be added, he said, with additional tickets going on sale next week.
"I cannot hide how I feel anymore": Ed Sheeran addresses Macklemore row at show
While performing as the opening act for Sheeran at a concert in early September in New Jersey, Macklemore said: "A big part of the reason why I wanted to do this tour in the first place is so that I could stand up in stadiums like this and say two words that are very, very dear to my heart: Free Palestine."
The Thrift Shop rapper then performed a song dedicated to pro-Palestinian protesters at Columbia University.
After he was taken off the tour on 14 September, Macklemore accused stadium owners of rallying together to push him out. He was also accused by billionaire stadium owner Robert Kraft of hate speech and antisemitic rhetoric surrounding Israel and Gaza.
Sheeran early on said that the decision to drop Macklemore from his tour was made by concert promoter Messina Touring Group.
His early remarks led to all of his support acts to drop out of the tour in solidarity, and fans to express frustration. Ticket prices for the tour plummeted as well.
Sheeran addressed the controversy head-on during the start of his set in Philadelphia last week.
He said he had made "mistakes" handling the fallout, apologising to fans and taking a stand on the Israel-Gaza conflict, which he said was "a humanitarian issue".
He described the 7 October 2023 Hamas-led attacks as "horrific", and also called the situation in Gaza "unjustifiable and disproportionate".

articles.title_orig: Dolly Parton's sister defends iconic singer's nephew over restraining order: 'We all love Bryan.'
articles.title_zh: Dolly Parton's sister defends iconic singer's nephew over restraining order: 'We all love Bryan.'
articles.content_orig:
One of Dolly Parton's sisters has defended the singer's nephew, Bryan Seaver, after he was fired by the music icon's estate and became the subject of a temporary restraining order.
Freida Parton, Dolly's younger sister, said the family was united in a statement on Instagram while showing support for Seaver, who is her sister Cassie Parton's son.
"Hi I'll say this and this only: there is no feud within our family. No one among the Parton/Owens family is fighting over Dolly's estate," she wrote. "We all love Bryan, just as we love each other. I love you all!!"
Her comments follow a Tennessee judge granting Parton's estate a temporary restraining order against Seaver on Wednesday, according to the Associated Press, the latest twist in the ongoing saga over her legacy.
On Tuesday, She's Alive LLV, the entity run by Parton's longtime manager Danny Nozell, submitted a legal filing seeking the order against Seaver and his private security company, accusing him of threatening to commit violence and destroy his aunt's legacy.
In court documents filed in Nashville, She's Alive LLC claimed that Seaver, who worked as Parton's head of security, sent increasingly threatening text messages in the weeks before and after the singer's death. The Associated Press , Variety and The New York Times published excerpts of the messages contained in the court filing.
In one of the texts dated Sept. 1, Seaver threatened to "set up a podcast dedicated to ruining Dolly's brand partnerships and telling the violations these people have done on us."
"It's going to be great," Seaver wrote. "Or f***ing pay me."
In other texts, Seaver threatened to "ratf*** every entity" that helps operate Parton's estate, saying he would become "the hand of retribution for my entire family."
Seaver also described himself as a "killer" and "an international arms dealer and mercenary," according to the court documents.
His security company, Squadron Augmented Protection Services, "was not a conventional office-security operation," the filing stated. "It was a heavily armed, paramilitary-style force."
A hearing on whether to extend the restraining order is scheduled for Oct. 7.
Parton died on Aug. 25 after a "brief battle with cancer," her publicist said. She was 80. Seaver announced her death in an Instagram video , saying his aunt had picked him to do it "years ago."
"It is an honor, an honor that is mixed with absolute pride and great sadness. But sadness lies with us, not with Dolly," Seaver said.
Seaver was fired by Parton's estate last week. According to the filing, Seaver's "terrorizing conduct made their continued retention untenable." The restraining order prevents Seaver and his company from talking with or being within 1,000 feet of She's Alive employees, attorneys and business partners.
In a statement to TMZ , Seaver said the messages included in the filing were taken out of context.
"I am a career soldier and military contractor and do conduct arms deals for foreign governments. I am a security professional and I am a killer," Seaver said. "However, nothing in this lawsuit were threats and most of the comments I stand by."
"I was talking frankly in a private way with Danny who I thought was my friend and he fancies himself a gangster," he added. "A lot of these messages are two guys having rage talk and crying on the phone together while we were grieving."

articles.title_orig: Big business warns Trump against diesel export ban in joint letter
articles.title_zh: Big business warns Trump against diesel export ban in joint letter
articles.content_orig:
The biggest business groups in the U.S. warned President Trump against a diesel export ban this week, saying in a joint letter that such an action would prove counterproductive and raise fuel prices rather than  lower them.
The U.S. Chamber of Commerce, Business Roundtable, National Association of Manufacturers, American Petroleum Institute and dozens of other groups told Trump that an export ban would "lead to less fuel production, tighter supplies and rising costs for American families, farmers and truckers."
"You have been asked by some to ban or limit the export of diesel to help lower prices, when in fact the opposite would occur," the groups warned in the letter sent to Trump on Wednesday.
You can download the letter here
Trump is facing growing political pressure from Republican lawmakers in farm states including Iowa to take action to lower fuel prices ahead of the U.S. midterm elections. Diesel cost a national average of $6.51 per gallon Thursday, $2.82 more expensive than the same period last year, according to data from AAA.
Trump said Tuesday that he has advocated for an export ban during deliberations within the administration. The remarks took the oil industry and business groups by surprise.
"I've said let's not send out the diesel. We make a lot of diesel," Trump told reporters on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly in New York. "I've called for it within my people. I've been talking about it."
Asked by Trump to explain the administration's deliberations to the press, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the White House was examining whether an export ban is "feasible in terms of the overall refining capacity and whether a full or partial ban would work."
A report on Politico Wednesday citing unnamed sources that the administration was preparing a plan to ban diesel exports for 90 days drove down diesel futures and shares of U.S. oil refiners.
But U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright told The New York Times later Wednesday that "nobody wants a full blanket ban or zero exports of diesel."
"That's not being discussed," Wright told the Times. "What's being discussed is what's the most efficient way to get more diesel into the United States of America and continue maximum flows of gasoline and jet fuel and all that."
Wright, an oil industry veteran who previoulsy served as CEO of oilfield servicer Liberty Energy , has said a diesel export ban would raise U.S. gasoline prices.
Energy experts say an export ban would lead to a brief collapse in diesel prices in some U.S. regions but fuel prices would then shoot higher as refiners cut production in response to the restrictions.
Diesel prices have soared as Ukraine's attacks on Russian refineries have forced Moscow to ban diesel exports. Russia was previously the second-largest diesel exporter in the world. A ban on U.S. diesel exports would remove the global market's largest source of supply.
Iran and its Houthi allies have also attacked refineries in the Middle East, and exports through the Strait of Hormuz are constrained as Iran continues to threaten and attack tankers.

articles.title_orig: Saudi Arabia Downs Houthi Missiles Targeting Kingdom, Official Says
articles.title_zh: Saudi Arabia Downs Houthi Missiles Targeting Kingdom, Official Says
articles.content_orig:
Saudi-led coalition forces fighting Yemen’s Houthis say they have intercepted six ballistic missiles allegedly fired by the Iran-allied group towards cities in Saudi Arabia.
The missiles were destroyed on Thursday in the direction of the Saudi cities of Taif and the strategically important port of Yanbu, according to Major General Turki al-Malki, the spokesman for the Saudi-backed Coalition to Restore Legitimacy in Yemen.
Saudi air defences intercepted some of the missiles attempting to target the cities, Al-Malki told the Saudi Press Agency (SPA).
There was no immediate claim of responsibility from the Houthis or other groups.
The coalition statement came as the Reuters news agency reported that an ‌‌air defence system operated by Greek ⁠⁠military ⁠⁠personnel in Saudi Arabia intercepted a ballistic missile and a drone on Thursday in ⁠⁠the wider Yanbu region, home to major oil refining facilities.
“Both were shot down,” a Greek security source told Reuters, adding that the Greek Patriot system launched two missiles but did not give details ⁠⁠on the origin of the ⁠⁠drone and the ballistic missile. A second source confirmed the information to the news agency.
Yanbu port is key to Saudi crude when shipments through the Strait of Hormuz are disrupted.
Earlier on Thursday, Saudi Arabia’s General Directorate of Civil Defence issued alerts warning of potential danger in the holy city of Mecca, the northwestern area of Tabuk, the Red Sea areas of Jeddah and Yanbu and the southern area of Taif. They later said the threat had passed and the cities were out of danger.
Last week, Saudi Arabia said it intercepted a drone launched by the Houthis towards Mecca , an accusation the group strongly denied, with Houthi leader Abdel-Malik al-Houthi calling the Saudi claims “a heinous lie”.
It was the first time in nearly 10 years that a security alert had been activated in Mecca, home to the Kaaba, Islam’s holiest site.
The Houthis have largely attacked southern areas of Saudi Arabia.
They stepped up attacks on the kingdom after declaring a naval blockade in July, a second theatre for the US-Iran war. The Houthis also seized the whole of Yemen’s western coast in a lightning offensive nearly two weeks ago that brought them to the shores of the Red Sea’s strategic Bab al-Mandeb waterway.
Forces with Yemen’s Saudi-backed internationally recognised government said on Thursday they repelled Houthi attacks along several fronts in Yemen’s southwestern Taiz governorate.
Colonel Majid al-Nuzaili, spokesman for the Yemeni government forces, said that the Houthis launched coordinated attacks on Wednesday night in a bid to reach positions on a key road connecting the Aden, Lahj and Taiz governorates.

articles.title_orig: Rare September Nor’easter set to slam East Coast with heavy rain, damaging winds
articles.title_zh: Rare September Nor’easter set to slam East Coast with heavy rain, damaging winds
articles.content_orig:
Millions across the Northeast are bracing for an intense, multi-day Nor’easter this weekend that is forecast to bring heavy rain and strong wind gusts to the East Coast.
Forecast models still disagree on the storm’s exact track, but one thing is clear: wherever it goes, it will hit the region hard. Forecasters have high confidence in a long-duration onshore wind event that could bring significant coastal flooding.
Coastal flood warnings and high wind watches are already in place along much of the East Coast, with more alerts likely to be issued throughout the day Thursday.
The highest rainfall totals — 2 to 3 inches or more — are most likely from Rhode Island to eastern Massachusetts.
Powerful winds, including gusts up to 50-60 mph, risk toppling power lines and trees. Small shifts in the storm’s track will determine where outages and downed trees are most likely to occur.
Coastal flooding is expected to run 1 to 3 feet above high tide, and a full moon Saturday night could intensify the tides and worsen the flooding. Waves along the coast are expected to reach 12 feet in Ocean City, New Jersey, and up to 22 feet in New England.
Moderate to major flooding is likely from North Carolina to Nantucket, Massachusetts, with southeastern Virginia — particularly the Virginia Beach-to-Norfolk area — at highest risk for major coastal inundation of 1 to 3 feet.
Meanwhile, a separate storm is already pummeling the Eastern Seaboard, generating high winds and rough surf.
In Massachusetts, residents were seen this week hauling their boats out of the bay, worried about high tides and flooding from the Nor’easter. One person told NBC News he’d been “prepping all week for both wind and water.”
One couple even changed their wedding plans because of the storm — they had been set to marry this weekend on a Massachusetts beach.
And the Boston Red Sox moved Sunday’s game — the season finale — up to Friday to avoid any weather-related delays or cancellations.
In New Jersey, crews cleared debris from storm drains and flood-prone areas as emergency management officials urged residents to prepare for the incoming storm. Monmouth County Sheriff Shaun Golden recommended charging devices and stocking up on batteries ahead of possible power outages.
Elsewhere in the country, days of heavy rain in the Southwest have triggered major flooding, sending muddy waters sweeping through the streets of New Mexico. The El Paso, Texas, fire department said it has responded to more than 50 storm-related calls.
Off the coast of Hawaii’s Big Island, Tropical Storm Nolo threatens heavy rain and flash flooding, with more than 30 inches of rain  possible in some areas. Extreme rainfall remains the storm’s biggest risk.
Nolo currently has sustained winds of 50 mph and is expected to strengthen into a hurricane by Thursday night — potentially reaching Category 3 strength. As of the latest update, the storm was about 285 miles south of South Point, Hawaii, moving north at 2 mph.
Nolo is not expected to make direct landfall in Hawaii, but it could come close enough to bring tropical-storm-force winds to the Big Island and Maui as early as Thursday night, with hurricane-force winds possible by Friday night.

articles.title_orig: Week 4 college football viewer's guide: Loaded Saturday slate features 6 games between ranked teams, including Texas at Tennessee
articles.title_zh: Week 4 college football viewer's guide: Loaded Saturday slate features 6 games between ranked teams, including Texas at Tennessee
articles.content_orig:
Week 4 is the biggest weekend of the 2026 college football season.
Saturday features six matchups between teams ranked in the AP Top 25. Four of those come in the SEC and the other two are in the Big Ten. We won't filibuster any longer. Here are the games to watch this weekend.
The winner gets to be called UT for the rest of the year. The loser has to find another acronym.
It's the biggest game of young Tennessee QB Faizon Brandon's career and he's shown why he won the starting QB job as a true freshman through the first three games. Brandon has yet to throw an interception and has nine total touchdowns; he's thrown for six and rushed for three.
Two of those games have come against Furman and Kennesaw State , so it's hard to judge just how good the Volunteers offense actually is this season. But it's a promising sign that Tennessee has been able to dominate its opponents on the ground no matter who it has played. In a 45-24 win over Georgia Tech , the Vols rushed 45 times for 299 yards.
That takes pressure off Brandon; he was 10-of-21 passing for 148 yards and two scores against the Yellow Jackets. Is that run game sustainable against the Longhorns? Teams are averaging just 3.4 yards a carry against Texas this season and Ohio State had 94 yards on 31 carries.
Auburn transfer Cam Coleman hasn't caught more than four passes in a game so far the season for Texas, but he's scored twice against both Texas State and UTSA. Arch Manning is averaging under seven yards an attempt through the first three games of the season and Tennessee's opponents have thrown for just 453 yards all season.
The Rebels' status as an underdog isn't a sign of disrespect to a top-five team. Rather, it's more about how good Florida has looked through the first three weeks of Jon Sumrall's tenure.
The Gators were the clear better team in their win over Auburn as Jadan Baugh has established himself as one of the best running backs in the country. Baugh has 458 yards and eight touchdowns already this season and is averaging 8.5 yards every time he carries the ball. Teams haven't been afraid to run the ball against Ole Miss so far this season, either. Charlotte's 33 attempts are the fewest of any Ole Miss opponent and LSU rushed for 172 yards and two scores in the Rebels' 32-24 win in Week 3.
It's also a potential letdown spot for Ole Miss. The game against LSU was such a focal point since the schedule was released that it's only natural to think the Rebels won't be as up for this game. Will that be rooted in any basis in reality? We'll know on Saturday.
We may also need to wait until Saturday to know about Ole Miss RB Kewan Lacy 's status. He re-injured his surgically repaired left shoulder in the win over LSU and missed the end of the game. JT Lindsey was effective in Lacy's absence, but Ole Miss is a much better football team with its star on the field. Having Lacy out there and effective helps Trinidad Chambliss share the playmaking burden.
This game has all the potential in the world to satiate your desires for old-school football. The over/under of 38.5 is the lowest of any game offered at BetMGM in Week 4.
No one is giving up fewer points per game than Iowa through three weeks. The Hawkeyes have shut out Northern Illinois and Northern Iowa — at least Michigan doesn't have "north" in its name — and allowed 13 points to Iowa State in Week 2. Those three teams have put up just 177 yards per game.
Hank Brown has taken over as Iowa's starting quarterback after a competition with Jeremy Hecklinski that went all the way to Week 1. The former Auburn QB is 45-of-62 passing for 473 yards and three touchdowns. Those are explosive numbers compared to the passing offense that Iowa has had in recent seasons.
The biggest question may actually come at running back, where both Kamari Moulton and L.J. Phillips missed the Week 3 win. Moulton and Phillips are the Hawkeyes' top running backs. Iowa didn't need them against its FCS foe, but will need at least one available on Saturday.
Michigan's offense finally broke free in the second half of a 52-17 win over UTEP in Week 3. After scoring 30 points over the first two weeks of the season, the Wolverines nearly matched that number with four touchdowns in the third quarter alone.
Will that game be a turning point for an offense that had looked stuck for the better part of 10 quarters? There are few questions about the Michigan defense. The ceiling for the Wolverines will be entirely determined by just how good the offense can be.
Some of the luster disappeared from this game as both teams lost in Week 3. Texas A&M's home loss to Kentucky was entirely unexpected. And it wasn't a fluke, either. The Wildcats bossed the Aggies .
Texas A&M lost receiver Terry Bussey for the season with a right leg injury on the opening kickoff. That puts more pressure on Mario Craver and Isaiah Horton to be the primary playmakers for an Aggies passing game that looks to need a robust support system around quarterback Marcel Reed . Craver and Horton have combined to catch 31 of the 62 completions Reed has thrown this season and all but one of his touchdown passes.
Reed emerged as Texas A&M's quarterback in this game two seasons ago as he came off the bench to rush for three scores in a 38-23 win. This season, he's completing less than 60% of his passes.
Sam Leavitt is still looking for his first great game as LSU's starting quarterback. Leavitt has thrown at least one interception in each of the Tigers' first three games and has five interceptions to just three touchdown passes. He's supplemented that total with six rushing touchdowns, but Leavitt needs to be a better passer for the Tigers' playoff hopes to become reality.
And the playoff is going to be a central theme of this game. The loser will drop to 2-2 and likely have no path to the postseason with another loss.
This is another game with some serious playoff implications, especially for an Oregon team that already has a loss thanks to that Week 2 defeat at Oklahoma State.
Even if it'd be a victory over a .500 Oregon team, a win would be a defining one for this Big Ten version of USC. The Trojans haven't threatened to be in the top tier of the conference since making the move from the Pac-12. Yes, there was a home win over Michigan in 2025, but that Wolverines team finished with five losses.
As always, there are still questions about the USC defense. The Trojans shut out Fresno State in a dominant Week 1 performance. But they've otherwise allowed 26 points in each of the other three games and 75 points combined over the past two weeks. The 35 points Rutgers scored in Week 3 was just seven fewer than the Scarlet Knights ' combined total over the first two weeks of the season.
If Oregon's offense has the same tells that it allegedly did against Oklahoma State, former TCU coach Gary Patterson's unit can tee off. But if the Portland State game was some much-needed corrective action, the Ducks could easily be the third straight team to drop 30 or more against the Trojans. If that happens and USC still wins, QB Jayden Maiava is going to get a lot of Heisman love. Through four games, Maiava is completing 76% of his passes for 1,173 yards and 12 TDs to just one interception.

articles.title_zh: Googlebooks will get full GeForce Now support ‘later this year’
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia says Google’s new Gemini-infused laptops are slated to get GeForce Now support before the year is up, which is perfect because Googlebooks don’t exactly pack a ton of power.
The entire Googlebook line was officially announced on September 21, spanning across Acer, Dell, ASUS, HP, and Lenovo. Each has its own draw, but they share the same baseline 16GB of RAM, up to 32GB. Each is equipped with a touchscreen and made from “premium materials,” and they genuinely look great. What qualifies as “premium” ranges from aluminum to carbon fiber. Of course, each has the instantly iconic Glowbar somewhere on the cover, flashing when the laptop is opened or closed.
In essence, Googlebooks run Android, for better or worse. Googlebook OS is almost a parallel operating system, but it and mobile Android go hand-in-hand by design. By nature, that means Google didn’t intend to pack these with discrete graphics cards that could power most games. But that’s why GeForce Now exists, right?
Nvidia announced that GeForce Now would be coming to Googlebooks in an official capacity before the year is up. The original statement only specifies it will arrive “later this year,” which leaves a gap of around three months.
That doesn’t mean GeForce Now won’t work with Googlebooks when they become available in October. Google Chrome and even Firefox now support GeForce Now natively through the browser. That means logging into the game streaming website will present a similar experience to a fully dedicated Googlebook app.
Still, an app will likely be a better experience tailored to the hardware outfit Google and its partners pack into the new laptops.
This was expected for a couple of reasons. Google has partnered with Nvidia in the past, and Chromebooks were one of the main targets for GeForce Now in the early days. On top of that, when Googlebooks were first shown off, the majority of titles seen were via GeForce Now and not running on native hardware.

articles.title_orig: Stabbing at Catholic convent in Poland leaves 1 person dead and 4 wounded
articles.title_zh: Stabbing at Catholic convent in Poland leaves 1 person dead and 4 wounded
articles.content_orig:
One person was killed and four others injured when a man armed with a knife attacked clergy and worshippers at a Catholic monastery in southern Poland.
Police said the 31-year-old attacker, a Ukrainian national, went on a stabbing spree at the 17th-century Benedictine abbey in Jaroslaw, some 30km (19 miles) from the border with Ukraine, on Thursday morning.
The suspect, who had entered Poland from Germany earlier in the day, reportedly grabbed a knife from the abbey’s kitchen and attacked four men and one woman, including a priest in a confessional, police said.
“Three of the victims are clergy members and two are laypeople; one person has died,” said prosecutor Bozena Harasz-Wołoszyn. Two others were in “critical, life-threatening condition”.
Polish media identified the man who died as a priest. Police did not immediately confirm the identity of the deceased.
Prosecutors said the attacker was headed for a nearby border crossing back into Ukraine but instead went to the abbey.
The motive remains unclear, and doctors will assess whether he was under the influence of alcohol, Harasz-Wołoszyn said.
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said the “murderer” would be “punished with the full severity of Polish law”.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called the attack a “horrific crime”.
“The perpetrator of this evil must bear full responsibility in accordance with the law … We are shaken by this evil. Justice must be done.”
The mayor of Jaroslaw, Marcin Nazarewicz, declared a period of mourning until the end of the week.
Stabbings, particularly at religious sites, are extremely rare in Poland, one of Europe’s most Catholic countries.

Swift revealed “The Life of a Showgirl: The Encore” on Wednesday after announcing “Patient Zero” the day before. The album, an expanded version of last year’s “The Life of a Showgirl,” includes four new tracks: “Patient Zero,” “Cleveland!,” “Pink Clouding” and “Babylon.”

articles.title_orig: Fury vs Joshua: Cardiff to host heavyweight fight on 11 December
articles.title_zh: Fury vs Joshua: Cardiff to host heavyweight fight on 11 December
articles.content_orig:
Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua have not shared a ring since a sparring session in 2010
Anthony Joshua and Tyson Fury will contest their long-awaited all-British heavyweight fight at Cardiff's Principality Stadium on 11 December.
The bout, more than a decade in the making, will be broadcast globally on Netflix.
BBC Sport understands the main event could take place in the early hours of Saturday morning in the UK, with organisers considering a late start to cater for audiences in the United States.
Joshua and Fury will come face-to-face at a news conference in London on Wednesday, 30 September, as the build-up begins to one of the most anticipated fights in British boxing history.
"I am inspiring a generation," Joshua, 36, posted on Instagram. Fury, 38, is yet to comment on the announcement.
The event is being promoted as a collaboration between Saudi boxing powerbroker Turki Alalshikh's The Ring and UFC chief Dana White.
"Two of the best heavyweights of this generation, finally in the ring together," Alalshikh said.
"This will be one of the biggest fights in boxing history. I am very happy to make this fight happen for the fans."
The former two-time world champions had already signed contracts for the bout earlier this year, but the date and venue had yet to be confirmed.
London's Wembley Stadium and New York's Madison Square Garden were the frontrunners to stage the fight, but both presented issues before Cardiff recently emerged as an alternative.
The Principality Stadium has hosted late-night boxing before, including Joe Calzaghe's fight with Mikkel Kessler in November 2007, which began at 01:00 GMT.
Welsh Rugby Union and Cardiff Council officials welcomed the fight, saying it would reinforce the city's reputation for staging major events and could bring a significant economic boost, although some operational details still need to be finalised.
Joshua had been pushing for the fight to take place in the UK and has got his wish.
"Forever indebted to the UK public for their support of Anthony Joshua. We couldn't have got this over the line without you," his promoter Eddie Hearn said.
It is notable that White, who fronts Zuffa Boxing, is involved in the promotion.
"For more than a decade, boxing fans have been clamouring for the heavyweight showdown between Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua. Together, they bring 66 wins, 52 knockouts and multiple heavyweight world titles into the ring," White said.
"On December 11, two of the biggest heavyweights of this generation finally collide - and the winner will take a significant place in heavyweight history."
There was no official statement from Hearn or Fury's promoter Frank Warren in the official news release sent by Netflix. Hearn had previously said he did not want White to be involved in promoting the fight.
'None of this is unusual' - Warren on AJ v Fury fight timings
A major fight in Cardiff taking place in the early hours might seem unusual, but there is precedent for UK events being scheduled around American television audiences.
Ricky Hatton's career-defining victory over Kostya Tszyu at Manchester's MEN Arena in June 2005 began at about 02:00 local time, allowing US broadcaster Showtime to show the fight on Saturday evening.
Less than a year later, Welshman Calzaghe's unification fight against Jeff Lacy at the same arena was staged at a similar hour. Calzaghe's 2007 victory over Kessler in Cardiff was also influenced by the US television schedule.
Mixed martial arts has gone even later. Michael Bisping's UFC title defence against Dan Henderson in Manchester in 2016 began deep into the night, with the fighters making their way to the octagon at about 04:45 local time.
When the UFC returned to Manchester in 2024, the UFC 304 main card began at 03:00 BST - corresponding with its traditional 22:00 start on the US east coast, with Briton Leon Edwards fighting Belal Muhammad in the main event just after 05:30.
The precise timing of Fury-Joshua has yet to be announced and promoter Eddie Hearn has played down suggestions it could begin as late as 03:00 GMT.
A ringwalk around 01:00 or 02:00 GMT would place the fight at 20:00 or 21:00 respectively on the US east coast.
'I think Tyson will knock Joshua out'
For years, British boxing has debated who would win, watched negotiations collapse and wondered whether Fury and Joshua would ever actually share a ring.
Now, finally, there is a date and a venue. It's happening.
In many ways, the uncertainty of recent weeks was the Fury-Joshua story of the past decade in miniature.
In 2020, the two camps agreed the basis of a two-fight deal. In 2021, contracts were signed for an undisputed heavyweight contest, only for Deontay Wilder's successful arbitration case to force Fury into a third fight with the American. Then, in 2022, Joshua accepted a 60-40 split to challenge Fury, but that attempt also fell apart.
Joshua gets the British fight he wanted, organisers are given a stadium capable of staging a huge event in December and broadcasters can tailor it towards American audiences.
There is also an intriguing subplot in White's involvement. While it does not necessarily tell us who wielded the most influence behind the scenes, his involvement underlines just how many powerful figures were involved in finally putting this fight together.
What matters most for supporters is that Fury-Joshua will happen in Britain. There are some fights that are about more than purses, broadcast deals and site fees. This is one of them.
British fans have followed every twist: the world-title wins, the defeats, the comebacks, the rivalries and, above all, the failed attempts to make this contest.
Now they will have the chance to travel to Wales and say they were there. Tens of thousands will descend on the Principality Stadium for what will be one of the biggest nights British boxing has staged in years.
And somewhere among them may be a youngster attending their first fight, watching two of Britain's most recognisable sportsmen make their walks to the ring and deciding they want to lace up a pair of gloves themselves.
The fight may have arrived years later than many wanted but Fury-Joshua can still leave that kind of legacy.

Sen. Bernie Sanders went after President Donald Trump’s star-studded dinner with Chinese President Xi Jinping, accusing the tech titans on the guest list of getting richer while Americans face an uncertain future with artificial intelligence.
“Trump invited 10 Big Tech Oligarchs to his private dinner with President Xi of China,” the Vermont independent wrote on X.

Sen. Mark Warner, D-Va., announced plans to introduce a Senate bill requiring mandatory pre-release safety testing for artificial intelligence models .
Basic cyber standards and safety protocols for AI test beds are an urgent necessity supported by major U.S. corporations, not just tech companies, Warner told reporters Thursday .
"We can debate about data centers, kids safety, AI liability, but let's at least do a pre-model release safety testing," Warner said. Enterprise real estate teams manage massive amounts of operational data, but it is often fragmented across disconnected spreadsheets, static tools, and expensive consultancies.
Trebellar provides an AI-native platform that unifies lease, occupancy, and market data into a single system of record. Its AI agents can run predictive analytics, generate instant reports, and recommend agile cost-saving measures tailored to a company's portfolio.
With participation from investors like Haystack and Alt Capital, Trebellar plans to expand its engineering teams, go-to-market efforts, and AI capabilities. The platform is already being utilized by major enterprise clients, including Meta, Uber, and Merck.

Xi said the competition between the U.S. and China should be a "healthy one, and should be kept within bounds."

Xi remarks came during a White House visit on his summit with President Donald Trump in  Washington. Xi and Trump entered the Oval Office for private talks thereafter.
A bipartisan group of senators is reportedly introducing a new transparency bill Thursday that would legally require artificial intelligence companies to disclose how their models operate and what internal safeguards are in place to prevent misuse.
The measure is spearheaded by Sens. Chris Coons, D-Del.; Katie Britt, R-Ala.; Brian Schatz, D-Hawaii; and James Lankford, R-Okla., Semafor reported Wednesday.
The legislation taps the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) to oversee and enforce the new disclosure requirements for AI developers.
While other lawmakers have pitched sweeping proposals — such as outright bans on " superintelligence " or massive economic overhauls — this bill takes a more modest, targeted approach focused strictly on public awareness and operational transparency.
"Americans deserve to know what [AI companies] are actually doing to place safety guardrails on large AI models," Coons said in a statement announcing the push, according to the report.
Google will load a refrigerator-sized satellite onto a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket Oct. 1, marking the tech giant's first concrete step toward building solar-powered artificial intelligence data centers in orbit.
Built in a rushed partnership with Planet Labs, "Project Suncatcher" is a "MVP" (minimum viable product) satellite contains four specialized tensor processing units (TPUs) — roughly the computing power of a single Earth-bound server.
Unfurling solar panels will supply one kilowatt of power to run the system.
Because traditional cooling fans are useless in the vacuum of space, Google engineers developed a custom thermal interface using conductive putty, copper, and aluminum to radiate heat outward.
The chips can process simple Gemini queries for 15 minutes before needing to shut down and cool off.

articles.title_orig: Krasnodar Region Declares State of Emergency as Ukrainian Strikes Cripple Grain Exports
articles.title_zh: Krasnodar Region Declares State of Emergency as Ukrainian Strikes Cripple Grain Exports
articles.content_orig:
Southern Russia’s Krasnodar region has declared a state of emergency following weeks of intense Ukrainian strikes against Black Sea ports and shipping infrastructure, which have hobbled export routes and left local farms overflowing with unsold grain, authorities said.
Both Russia and Ukraine have stepped up attacks on the other's grain vessels in the Black Sea in recent months, sending global prices higher.
Krasnodar region Governor Veniamin Kondratyev signed the emergency decree on Wednesday, retroactively setting its effective date to Aug. 12. The order cites “mass attacks on logistics facilities, suspended port operations and disrupted shipping in the Azov-Black Sea basin ” as the reason for emergency measures.
In August, Ukrainian drone and missile strikes were estimated to have taken 90% of Russia’s grain export capacity in the region offline, according to industry analysts. The vast majority of the country’s agricultural shipments flow out of the Azov-Black Sea basin.
Kondratyev said many farmers in the Krasnodar region have been unable to sell their grain, leading to an oversupply that threatens to “disrupt normal living conditions for the population and cause significant material losses.”
The Krasnodar region, one of Russia’s primary agricultural hubs, has seen a very productive harvest this year, with total grain yields projected to outpace last year’s output.
Disruptions to export infrastructure have created a surplus of grain in the domestic market , leading to lower prices in Russia and unsold inventories.
The Central Bank warned this week that prolonged disruptions to grain export routes could negatively impact agricultural output in the future.
Russia is seeking to reroute its agricultural exports away from the Black Sea through its Baltic and Arctic ports, repurposing fertilizer and coal terminals to handle grain shipped by rail from southern Russia.
Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov held talks with U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Wednesday, after which Rubio said Ukraine and Russia had both voiced an interest in a limited ceasefire involving grain and energy-related targets.

Former "American Idol" contestant Caleb Flynn told his mistress he stayed up until 4 a.m. "literally thinking of ways to kill" his wife and "not go to jail," one of a series of messages read to jurors Thursday in his Ohio murder trial.
Alleigha Botner returned to the witness stand for a second day and walked jurors through months of messages in which Flynn allegedly talked repeatedly about wanting Ashley Flynn dead or gone.
In one May 2025 message, Flynn allegedly wrote, "If I could literally kill her and not go to hell, I would do it in a heartbeat."

Days later, he allegedly wrote, "I hate her, loathe her. I want her dead."

The messages became even more explicit in June, when Flynn allegedly told Botner, "Please hire someone to take [her] out. I need you in my life, I need you."
Botner responded: "So tempting. I can't live without you. And I've had this thought so often lately. How do we figure this out?"

Botner later became emotional before reading one of her own messages aloud.
"I want to kill her, Caleb," Botner wrote.
Alleigha Botner testifies Wednesday in the Ohio murder trial of former "American Idol" contestant Caleb Flynn. Prosecutors say Botner had an affair with Flynn before his wife, Ashley Flynn, was killed. (CREDIT: WKEF)
Flynn allegedly responded: "That makes two of us."
Flynn is accused of fatally shooting Ashley in the back of the head inside their home Feb. 16 before staging the scene to look like an intruder had broken in. He has pleaded not guilty to aggravated murder and other charges.
Botner had prefaced the message by telling jurors, "I just wish I didn't say this."
In the same August exchange, Flynn allegedly went on to write that he had been "literally trying to find a way to get rid of her, to be rid of her."
Botner responded that she was "not asking that you take her life, obviously," but said getting a divorce "would change everything."

For years, wanting GrapheneOS meant accepting one hardware choice: you needed a Google Pixel. Motorola’s partnership with the privacy-focused project promised to break that lock-in, but until now, we didn’t know which phone would go first. Following this week’s Signature 27 unveiling , GrapheneOS has answered that question directly: Motorola’s new flagship will be the first phone supported under the partnership.
The confirmation came after an X user asked whether the Signature 27 would support GrapheneOS. “Yes, that will be the initial supported phone. Wait for official news about it,” the project replied . That last sentence matters, since GrapheneOS has not yet announced when support will arrive or whether Motorola will offer the OS preinstalled.
Still, the choice makes sense. GrapheneOS previously explained what’s finally making Motorola support possible , noting that its first Motorola devices would be high-end flagships because Qualcomm’s top Snapdragon platforms currently provide the security features and long-term support it requires. The project has highlighted hardware memory tagging, stronger secure-element integration, and seven years of proper updates as key requirements.
The Signature 27 checks those boxes on paper. Motorola has equipped it with Qualcomm’s Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 and promised seven OS upgrades plus up to seven years of security updates. That lines up with GrapheneOS’s earlier roadmap, which pointed to a regular, non-folding flagship as the starting point before support expands to Motorola foldables.
The timing is especially interesting given GrapheneOS’s growing friction with Google. The project recently hit roadblocks bringing GrapheneOS to the Pixel 11 over MTE support. It has also criticized Google’s new manual process for accessing Pixel driver source code and accused the company of gatekeeping some Android 17 APIs and security fixes .
GrapheneOS is also preparing for life beyond Pixels on the software side. It is overhauling its Messaging app and planning native RCS support to reduce dependence on Google Messages, replacing aging AOSP apps, and rolling out privacy features such as secure paste.
So for anyone waiting for a serious non-Pixel GrapheneOS phone, the mystery is finally over. The Signature 27 is first in line.
